extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of images depicting complex everyday scenes of common objects in their natural context, with per-instance segmentation annotations.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin; Michael Maire; Serge Belongie; Lubomir Bourdev; Ross Girshick; James Hays; Pietro Perona; Deva Ramanan; C. Lawrence Zitnick; Piotr Dollar
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected primarily from Flickr using object-object and object-scene search queries to find non-iconic images, then filtered for validity and iconicity; annotations were gathered through a multi-stage Amazon Mechanical Turk pipeline for category labeling, instance spotting, segmentation, verification, and captions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Photos from Flickr retrieved via object-object and object-scene queries.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Candidate images were filtered to remove invalid or iconic images, near-duplicate images were explicitly removed, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates across splits.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation used a three-stage pipeline: category labeling with a hierarchical super-category interface, instance spotting of all instances for each category, and per-instance segmentation, followed by segmentation verification; five captions were also added per image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes annotation quality using expert comparison, precision/recall, majority vote ground truth, union of multiple AMT workers for recall, and verification voting for segmentations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling; 8 workers per image for instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for segmentation with 3 to 5 workers for verification; 5 captions per image
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk; expert workers were co-authors of the paper; children aged 4 to 8 were asked to name objects for category collection.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into 2014 and 2015 releases, with the first half released in 2014 and the cumulative second half in 2015; the dataset will evolve and grow over time, with up-to-date information online.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset emphasizes non-iconic images and excludes stuff categories; some categories were omitted from the 2014 release due to too many instances, ambiguity, confusion with other categories, or too few instances.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently labels only thing categories, not stuff; dense scenes with many instances are handled using crowd regions instead of individual instance segmentation; some categories were excluded from the 2014 release due to annotation difficulty or insufficient instances.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for object detection and instance segmentation in natural scenes; also intended to advance scene understanding and contextual reasoning.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. ... if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as “dog + car” we found many more non-iconic images. ... For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. ... To construct a high-quality set of non-iconic images, we first collected candidate images by searching for pairs of object categories, or pairs of object and scene categories.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We then created an AMT filtering task that allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates, Fig. 10. ... We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Our annotation pipeline is split into 3 primary tasks: (a) labeling the categories present in the image (§4.1), (b) locating and marking all instances of the labeled categories (§4.2), and (c) segmenting each object instance (§4.3). ... While the training task filtered out most bad workers, we also performed an explicit verification step on each segmented instance to ensure good quality. ... We added five written caption descriptions to each image in MS COCO.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT).

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: We analyzed crowd worker quality on the category labeling task by comparing to dedicated expert workers, see Fig. 4(a). ... Ground truth was computed using majority vote of the experts. ... Fig. 4(a) shows that the union of 8 AMT workers, the same number as was used to collect our labels, achieved greater recall than any of the expert workers. ... Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation and indicate whether it matched the instance well or not.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image. ... Each image was labeled by 8 workers for a total of ≈10k worker hours. ... To minimize cost we only had a single worker segment each instance. ... Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation ... We added five written caption descriptions to each image in MS COCO.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT). ... We compared precision and recall of seven expert workers (co-authors of the paper) ... several children ranging in ages from 4 to 8 were asked to name every object they see in indoor and outdoor environments.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: To accommodate a faster release schedule, we split the MS COCO dataset into two roughly equal parts. The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015. ... MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Since we are primarily interested in precise localization of object instances, we decided to only include “thing” categories and not “stuff.” ... Note that we have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories. We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Since we are primarily interested in precise localization of object instances, we decided to only include “thing” categories and not “stuff.” ... After 10-15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, the remaining instances were marked as “crowds” using a single (possibly multipart) segment. ... We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories ... (ambiguous and difficult to label) ... (too few instances).

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. ... The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images
